newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh oil barons stalling privatisation - PM.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh oil barons stalling privatisation - PM.

text.p: Kazakhstan's "oil barons" are resisting plans to privatise the former Soviet republic's potentially wealthy energy sector, Kazakh Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin said on Tuesday.
"The heads of state oil enterprises...do not want to go ahead with privatisation," Kazhegeldin told a group of diplomats and journalists in the Kazakh capital Almaty.
"But there has to be a proper owner, greater efficiency," he said.

The reformist prime minister is pushing forward an ambitious fast-track sell-off of state enterprises in Kazakhstan, a country dominated by steppe land five times the size of France, to raise cash to pay off a mountain of wage and pension arrears.
"We forecast privatisation to be completed by the end of 1997," Kazhegeldin said.
The plum in Kazakhstan's privatisation pie and the most attractive to foreign investors is the Central Asian state's troubled but reserve-rich oil and gas sector.

Nurlan Balgimbayev, the powerful head of state-owned oil concern Kazakh Oil, has said he wants to drag Kazakhstan from 26th place in terms of world crude oil output to sixth by 2010, with plans to pump 3.4 million barrels per day.

But Kazakhstan's so-called "oil barons," the enterprises' Soviet-era directors, are unwilling to hand over control to foreign companies despite a desperate need for foreign capital to arrest a plunge in output since independence in 1991.
Kazhegeldin's bull-like charge forward with oil privatisations came to an abrupt halt in March after President Nursultan Nazarbayev carried out a major shake-up of government structures.
Much of the real power in cutting oil deals fell from the hands of the prime minister and landed in the lap of Kazakh Oil's Balgimbayev.
On Tuesday, Kazhegeldin said he still maintained control over oil privatisations.

"The cash brought in by privatisation goes to the government and this cash is handled by the Ministry of Finance," Kazhegeldin said when asked who actually controlled oil privatisation. The finance ministry answers to Kazhegeldin.
But most Western oil executives and official sources in Almaty say real clout in the oil sell-offs now lies with Balgimbayev.
"There have been some jurisdictional changes," one Western advisor to the government said cautiously.

A recent government announcement of a tender for Embamunaigaz, the republic's fourth largest oil enterprise which produces about 256,000 barrels per day, was quietly shelved a week later by Balgimbayev.
